documents.abstract: Abstract Green chemistry seeks to prevent pollution at its source by reducing waste, energy demand, hazardous substances, and resource consumption. Artificial intelligence (AI), especially machine learning (ML), can strengthen this approach by learning from chemical and process data, predicting outcomes, screening large chemical spaces, and optimizing experiments. Recent literature identifies applications ranging from catalyst discovery and reaction optimization to CO₂ capture, sustainable polymers, waste management, water treatment, and process control. A 2026 review in Applied Intelligence highlights artificial neural networks, random forests, and Bayesian optimization as important approaches across these areas, while also emphasizing data quality, validation, energy use, and scalability as major concerns. (see References 1–6) This project reviews how AI can support the principles of green chemistry and proposes a practical research framework in which sustainability metrics are included directly in model objectives. The central idea is that an AI system should not merely maximize chemical yield; it should seek a balanced outcome involving yield, selectivity, waste, toxicity, energy, solvent impact, and resource efficiency. The report concludes that AI can become an enabling technology for greener chemistry when models are transparent, experimentally validated, and evaluated against environmental as well as technical performance.

Acute Care Surgery (ACS) emerged not as a single innovation, but as the progressive integration of operative discipline, intensive care, trauma systems, biologically informed resuscitation, and regionalized care infrastructure into a layered, complex, adaptive system. Artificial intelligence (AI) now represents the next major technological layer being introduced into this mature sociotechnical environment. This narrative review examines ACS from a systems perspective and argues that the success or failure of AI integration requires both algorithmic performance and how effectively these technologies couple with existing workflows, operational structures, feedback mechanisms, and clinical decision-making processes. Historical developments in ACS - including intensive care evolution, trauma system regionalization, damage control philosophy, and prior failures of reductionist biologic interventions - provide important lessons for understanding the opportunities and risks of AI deployment in high-acuity surgical care. Current AI applications in ACS include augmented diagnostics, continuous physiologic surveillance, predictive analytics, operative video analysis, workflow optimization, and educational assessment. However, important issues remain, including alert fatigue, automation bias, implementation failure, inequitable model generalizability, and the risks of introducing reductionist computational paradigms into complex adaptive systems. A systems-oriented framework emphasizes that AI tools must be evaluated not as isolated products, but as components of broader clinical, organizational, and educational ecosystems. ACS, with its longstanding experience integrating layered technologies and coordinating multidisciplinary care under conditions of uncertainty, may represent one of the most informative environments in which to study responsible AI implementation in surgery.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transitioning from a supportive tool to a core component of clinical decision-making in dentistry. This review synthesizes advances in deep learning and machine learning for oral disease diagnosis, orthodontic treatment prediction, pediatric oral health management, adolescent psychological-oral health interactions, and precision care for special-needs populations, drawing on evidence published predominantly between 2024 and 2026. A systematic search across PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus identified 30 studies for narrative synthesis. Several AI models reported higher diagnostic or predictive performance than selected conventional comparators in detecting periodontal bone loss, temporomandibular joint osteoarthritis, and oral squamous cell carcinoma, with accuracy frequently exceeding 90%. In orthodontics, AI-driven prediction reduces tooth movement error rates substantially. However, most studies rely on single-center retrospective data lacking prospective multicenter validation. Future priorities include multimodal data fusion, federated learning, and standardized validation frameworks to facilitate clinical translation.

Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in gastroenterology for endoscopic detection and characterisation, disease-activity assessment, risk prediction, treatment-response estimation and workflow support. However, high retrospective accuracy does not necessarily translate into reliable or beneficial clinical decision support. This structured narrative review examines the clinical development of artificial intelligence across gastrointestinal endoscopy, inflammatory bowel disease, hepatology and pancreaticobiliary diseases through three translational dimensions: explainability, generalisability and clinical actionability. Communication, human oversight and lifecycle governance are considered cross-cutting determinants of implementation. The evidence is most mature in gastrointestinal endoscopy, particularly for computer-aided polyp detection, although benefits vary across operators, indications and practice settings. Applications in inflammatory bowel disease, hepatology and pancreaticobiliary care remain predominantly retrospective, with limited prospective evidence that model outputs alter management or improve patient outcomes. Explainability is commonly represented by heatmaps or feature-attribution methods, but rarely evaluated in terms of clinician understanding, calibrated trust or patient communication. External validation is becoming more frequent, yet geographic and technological transportability, calibration and performance under dataset shift remain insufficiently assessed. Prospective implementation and health-economic studies are uncommon, and available economic evidence is largely model-based. Clinical artificial intelligence should therefore be evaluated as a sociotechnical intervention comprising the model, interface, users, workflow, communication process and associated care pathway. Translation requires clinically defined use cases, representative multicentre validation, human-centred evaluation, prospective assessment of benefits and harms, and continuous post-deployment surveillance. Clinical AI in gastroenterology should complement clinical expertise through transparent, contestable and continuously monitored decision support that preserves clinician accountability and supports informed, patient-centred decisions.

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) has rapidly become part of contemporary visual communication and is changing the way graphic designers generate, develop, refine, and present ideas. Tools based on generative AI can produce images, illustrations, layouts, typography suggestions, visual variations, and creative concepts within seconds. For graphic designers, this development offers significant opportunities for experimentation and efficiency, but it also raises important questions about creativity, originality, authorship, professional identity, and the future of design education. This paper explores the relationship between artificial intelligence and graphic design from the perspective of creative practice. The paper argues that AI does not eliminate the need for human creativity; instead, it changes where creative effort takes place. Designers increasingly need to formulate problems, evaluate generated possibilities, make cultural and aesthetic judgments, refine outputs, and give visual communication a meaningful human direction. At the same time, excessive dependence on AI may lead to design fixation, visual similarity, weakened foundational skills, and uncertainty regarding authorship. The paper concludes that the most productive future for graphic design lies in responsible human–AI collaboration, supported by strong foundations in design principles, visual thinking, ethics, and critical judgment.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the design industry by introducing data-driven, generative, predictive, and automated approaches to creative and technical processes. Interior design, traditionally dependent on human creativity, spatial understanding, material knowledge, and client preferences, is increasingly influenced by AI-powered tools capable of generating design concepts, visualizations, layouts, material combinations, lighting solutions, and personalized spatial recommendations. Recent developments in generative AI, machine learning, computer vision, natural language processing, and multimodal systems have expanded the possibilities for designers to explore a larger number of alternatives in less time. This research paper examines the opportunities, challenges, and future perspectives associated with the integration of Artificial Intelligence into interior design. The study adopts a qualitative systematic literature review approach and synthesizes recent research on AI-assisted architectural and built-environment design. The review indicates that AI can support concept generation, space planning, 3D visualization, material selection, sustainability analysis, personalization, and client communication. However, issues related to creativity, algorithmic bias, intellectual property, data privacy, professional responsibility, design authenticity, technical skills, and overdependence on automated systems remain significant challenges. Recent systematic reviews show that AI research in design is strongly concentrated in early conceptual and schematic stages, while later stages requiring detailed technical, contextual, and professional judgment remain comparatively underexplored. The paper argues that AI should not be viewed as a replacement for interior designers but as an augmentation technology that can strengthen human creativity, decision-making, and productivity. A human-centred AI framework combining technological capability with professional expertise, ethical safeguards, cultural sensitivity, and user participation is proposed. The study concludes that the future of interior design will increasingly depend on effective human–AI collaboration rather than complete automation.

Artificial intelligence (AI) supports the development of novel halal foods, including plant-based and cultivated alternatives, offering environmentally sustainable and cost-effective solutions to global food security challenges. While facilitating innovation and strengthening consumer trust, these advancements also raise significant ethical, regulatory, and religious concerns in Muslim contexts where compliance with Sharīʿah principles is essential. This study aims to examine how AI-enabled food innovations can align with Sharīʿah requirements while safeguarding halal integrity and consumer confidence. Employing a conceptual review methodology, the paper synthesizes Qur’anic and ḥadīth-based principles with contemporary scholarly literature and regulatory frameworks on AI integration, halal certification, and novel food governance. The study addresses a critical research gap concerning the absence of comprehensive Sharīʿah-based guidelines and harmonised regulatory standards for AI-driven novel foods, particularly in relation to certification, traceability, and consumer assurance. The analysis yields three key findings: (1) AI technologies enhance halal assurance systems through improved traceability, transparency, and risk management; (2) AI-enabled novel foods may be considered permissible under the concept of bidʿah ḥasanah (beneficial innovation) when their ingredients and production processes comply with established Sharīʿah principles; and (3) inadequate regulatory oversight and the lack of standardised certification frameworks pose risks to halal integrity and may erode consumer trust. The study concludes that responsible integration of AI in novel food innovation requires coupling technological advancement with robust Islamic ethical governance and recommends the development of harmonised standards through collaboration among halal authorities, policymakers, and industry stakeholders.

Abstract Surgical artificial intelligence (AI) is typically validated on one patient population and then deployed unchanged into another, without surgeon input into its design. AI in orthopaedics should be built with surgeons, not simply for them: Surgeons should hold shared authority over the clinical question, data curation, validation, implementation, monitoring and retirement of any tool they use. Specialty‐tuned models outperform general‐purpose systems on some tasks, but the margin is modest and likely to narrow as generalist models improve. The more durable distinction is who controls the update loop—who can retrain a model on local outcomes, audit its failures and withdraw it when it drifts. Trial evidence shows that a clinician kept in that loop by design, not as an afterthought, outperforms working alone. What determines whether orthopaedic AI fulfils its promise is not model architecture, but who stays accountable to the surgeon at the bedside when the model needs to change.

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is embedded in every financial transaction and interaction through robo-advising, auto- Recommendations, portfolios tracking, digital financial assistants, and financial information processing tools. This paper considers the relevance of AI to young investors of the Kalyan Region. Using relevant published evidence from SEBI, NSE, AMFI and RBI, along with peer-reviewed research and analysis, this paper applies descriptive, comparative and trend-oriented analysis to examine the use and impact of AI in personal finance management. Evidence shows an ageing-down of India's investor base, with young people constituting an increasing proportion of the registered individual investors. The study finds that AI can reduce information and access barriers and enable personalisation, monitoring, and analysis. However, the benefits are limited by financial literacy, trust, perceived risk, transparency and ability to question AI outputs.

Abstract The chemical industry is essential for modern society, but conventional chemical processes may require substantial quantities of energy, solvents and raw materials and can generate undesirable waste and emissions. Sustainable chemistry seeks to address these concerns by designing chemical products and processes that use resources more efficiently and reduce environmental and health risks. In parallel, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a powerful computational approach for analysing complex chemical information, predicting molecular and material properties, optimizing reactions and supporting scientific decision-making. The integration of AI with sustainable chemistry creates an opportunity to accelerate the development of safer, cleaner and more resource-efficient chemical technologies. This review examines the emerging role of AI in sustainable chemistry, with particular emphasis on machine learning, predictive modelling, reaction optimization, catalyst discovery, solvent selection, sustainable materials, carbon management, green hydrogen, waste valorization and analytical chemistry. The potential of AI to support the principles of green chemistry and life-cycle-based decision-making is also discussed. Recent studies indicate that AI can reduce experimental effort and improve the efficiency of chemical discovery and process development, although limitations related to data quality, interpretability, validation, computational requirements and industrial scale-up remain significant. The review further considers the relevance of AI-enabled sustainable chemistry to India's long-term development objectives under Viksit Bharat @2047. A future-oriented framework for responsible AI-driven chemistry is proposed, emphasizing scientific validation, environmental assessment, interdisciplinary collaboration and indigenous innovation.

Artificial intelligence plays a crucial role today by assisting providers in patient care and supporting them in various intelligent healthcare systems. The technique shifts from computational knowledge to machine learning, which can assess complex medical data. AI is ubiquitous in Healthcare, which can be used in treatment, diagnosis, patient risk identification, and predicting the outcome of clinical scenarios. An overview of different intelligent techniques presented in this article is discussed with the receiver of clinical application, and future challenges of the current scenario of AI in Healthcare. Articles and internet searches were carried out using the keywords Artificial Intelligence and computational Healthcare. Further references were obtained from Data available on Google Scholar, PubMed, medical databases, and cross-referencing from key articles based on it. The results are also assessed using a variety of quality standards, including prediction accuracy and rate, based on the examination of several papers on disease diagnosis.

documents.abstract: The aim of this study was to design and evaluate an artificial intelligence-driven teacher support system capable of translating multidimensional learning profiles into instructional and assessment recommendations for higher education. The proposal integrated five diagnostic dimensions: VARK, for preferences in accessing information; FSLSM, for processing and representation traits; ICAP, for levels of cognitive engagement; SRL, for self-regulated learning; and EBSI, for study habits. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods approach was used. In the quantitative phase, a digital questionnaire was administered to 145 students from five universities, and the data were processed through a system developed in Python, which generated diagnostic profiles and personalized pedagogical reports for teachers. In the qualitative phase, four instructors evaluated the usefulness, perceived coherence, feasibility, and ethical acceptability of the reports. The results showed substantial convergence between the diagnosis calculated without AI and the narrative generated with AI in dimensions such as VARK and ICAP, as well as favorable acceptance by the teaching staff. However, mismatches were identified in the calibration of FSLSM and in the intensity attributed to SRL and EBSI. It is concluded that AI can mediate instructional decision-making under pedagogical supervision

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping analytical chemistry by changing how instrumental measurements are processed, interpreted, optimized, and translated into chemical decisions. Modern analytical platforms generate high-dimensional spectra, chromatograms, mass spectra, images, and sensor signals in volumes that can exceed the practical capacity of conventional univariate or manually supervised workflows. This integrative review examines AI-driven advances across spectroscopy, chromatography, mass spectrometry, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), chemical sensors, imaging, and analytical method development. The review adopts a structured narrative design using purposive sampling of peer-reviewed reviews, primary methodological literature, and regulatory guidance identified through targeted searches of major biomedical and chemistry literature sources and official regulatory repositories. Evidence was thematically coded into four domains: data enhancement, predictive modelling, analytical-method optimization, and decision support. The synthesis indicates that machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), chemometrics, quantitative structure–retention relationships (QSRR), and hybrid mechanistic–data-driven approaches can improve pattern recognition, spectral deconvolution, analyte identification, retention prediction, calibration, anomaly detection, and experimental optimization when adequate and representative data are available. However, AI does not automatically create a valid analytical method: model leakage, biased sampling, poor external validation, instrument drift, explainability limitations, and weak uncertainty characterization can undermine apparent performance. Current regulatory thinking increasingly emphasizes risk-based credibility and conventional analytical validation principles. Future analytical laboratories are therefore likely to combine AI with robust metrology, automated experimentation, digital twins, explainable AI, multimodal data fusion, and continuous lifecycle validation. The central conclusion is that the strongest pathway is not replacement of analytical chemistry by AI, but integration of chemical knowledge, measurement science, and trustworthy computation.

The increasing use of artificial intelligence in audit practice has begun to reshape how audit tasks are performed, yet evidence on its implications for auditor performance remains limited, particularly in developing economies. This study investigates the relationship between artificial intelligence-driven audit technology and auditor performance in listed deposit money banks in Nigeria. Drawing on Task-Technology Fit Theory, AI-driven audit technology is examined through three functional dimensions, namely AI-based audit analytics, machine learning-enabled fraud detection systems, and robotic process automation in audit tasks, while auditor experience is incorporated as a control variable. The study employs a quantitative cross-sectional survey approach using data obtained from 410 audit professionals. Data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling with SmartPLS 4, following a two-stage procedure involving measurement and structural model assessment. The findings show that AI-based audit analytics, machine learning-enabled fraud detection systems, and robotic process automation each have a positive and statistically significant relationship with auditor performance. Auditor experience also demonstrates a significant positive influence, indicating that professional expertise complements, rather than replaces, the use of advanced audit technologies. Overall, the results provide empirical evidence that the effective alignment of technological capabilities with audit task requirements enhances auditor performance within the banking sector. The study contributes to auditing literature by offering evidence on the performance effects of disaggregated AI-driven audit technologies in a developing economy and highlights the practical importance of investing in both advanced audit tools and continuous professional development.

Background: Automated facial analysis has the potential to standardize orthodontic assessment by minimizing human error and variability. Prior work (Rousseau et al., 2022) compared AI-based and manual methods using only four landmarks and three ratios, leaving broader anthropometric evaluation unexplored.Objective: To validate an automated workflow that extracts sixteen facial landmarks, computes twenty-two anthropometric ratios and three vertical proportions from 2D clinical photographs, and to compare its reliability against manual measurements.Materials and Methods: One hundred patients (15–25 years) without craniofacial anomalies were enrolled. Two operators placed sixteen landmarks and computed all ratios and proportions twice to assess intra- and inter-rater reliability. The AI pipeline used a custom Python script integrating Mediapipe’s facial-landmark model. Reliability was quantified by intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs), and agreement between manual and AI measurements was examined via Bland–Altman analysis.Results: Manual intrarater ICCs exceeded 0.90 for 18 of 22 ratios and all vertical proportions, indicating excellent repeatability. Interrater ICCs were > 0.90 for seven ratios, 0.75–0.90 for ten, 0.50–0.75 for four, and < 0.50 for one; vertical-proportion ICCs ranged from 0.08 to 0.75. The AI workflow produced mean differences under 2 % compared to manual values, with 95 % of differences within Bland–Altman limits, demonstrating minimal systematic bias.Conclusions: The AI-driven method reliably reproduces manual anthropometric measurements across an expanded metric set, reducing operator variability and analysis time. This objective tool shows promise for standardized orthodontic evaluation. Future studies should test larger, multiethnic cohorts, extend to three-dimensional imaging, and assess routine clinical integration.

The rapid advancement of nanomedicine has improved drug delivery; however, conventional nanoparticle development remains limited by trial-and-error optimization, scalability constraints, and environmental concerns. Green nanotechnology offers a sustainable alternative through the use of biodegradable materials, renewable precursors, and environmentally benign synthesis approaches. Among emerging sustainable nanomaterials, green carbon dots have attracted increasing interest because of their biocompatibility, tunable surface chemistry, intrinsic fluorescence, and relatively low toxicity. Nevertheless, precise control of their physicochemical and biological properties remains challenging. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning and data-driven modeling, provides opportunities for predictive formulation design, optimization of nanocarrier properties, and reduction of experimental burden. The integration of AI with sustainable nanomedicine therefore offers a promising strategy for developing intelligent drug delivery systems with improved therapeutic precision, targeting, controlled drug release, and bioimaging capabilities. This review critically examines the convergence of AI and sustainable nanomedicine, with particular emphasis on green carbon dots for smart drug delivery. It discusses green synthesis strategies, AI-driven nanocarrier design and optimization, intelligent targeting, controlled drug delivery, bioimaging applications, and translational challenges. Future perspectives concerning scalability, reproducibility, regulatory considerations, and environmentally responsible manufacturing are also addressed, highlighting the potential of AI-enabled green carbon dots as a sustainable platform for next-generation drug delivery.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is fundamentally transforming accounting practice by displacing traditional data-processing tasks, augmenting auditing functions, and reshaping the professional competency requirements of financial reporting. While these technological developments generate substantial efficiency gains, they simultaneously introduce unprecedented ethical challenges, including algorithmic opacity, accountability diffusion, bias propagation in automated judgment, and the erosion of professional scepticism — that threaten the integrity of financial reporting and the public trust upon which the accounting profession's social licence to operate ultimately depends. This paper develops a rigorous, theoretically grounded analysis of the intersection between artificial intelligence and accounting ethics, drawing on institutional theory, agency theory, virtue ethics, and the stakeholder trust framework to diagnose how AI adoption reconfigures the ethical architecture of financial reporting and to prescribe the governance, professional, and regulatory responses required to safeguard ethical standards and trust in this transformed environment. The paper makes three original contributions: first, it develops a multi-dimensional taxonomy of AI-related ethical risks in accounting, distinguishing technical, professional, and systemic risk categories; second, it proposes the Ethical AI Accounting Governance Framework (EAAGF), an original implementation model that integrates algorithmic governance, professional ethics renewal, regulatory adaptation, and stakeholder assurance mechanisms; and third, it situates these contributions within a comparative empirical analysis of AI adoption experiences across major accounting contexts, integrating evidence from surveys, regulatory reports, and case illustrations. The paper argues that the central challenge is not whether AI will transform accounting — this is already occurring — but whether the profession, regulators, and organisations can collectively construct the ethical governance infrastructure required to ensure that transformation advances rather than undermines the accountability, transparency, and trust that constitute the profession's foundational social purpose.

documents.abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into multi-agent systems has shown great potential for automated debugging. Yet nearly all current frameworks rely on rigid, predefined architectures: the number of agents, their roles, and their interaction patterns are fixed before any analysis of the bug occurs. This one-size-fits-all approach is fundamentally mismatched to the heterogeneous nature of software defects. Simple bugs waste resources on unnecessary coordination, while complex ones suffer from insufficient or poorly aligned expertise. This paper introduces ASAD, an adaptive agentic system for debugging that configures its team according to the nature and complexity of each bug. ASAD initiates the debugging process by analyzing the faulty code and dynamically determines the number of agents to deploy, the specialized roles they should have, and the collaboration strategy they should follow. A central coordinator orchestrates this process through iterative planning, reflection, and execution; applying fast single-pass repairs for simple issues while assembling purpose-built teams to tackle more complex failures. We evaluate ASAD on three established benchmarks: Defects4J, DebugBench, and CodeFlaws, using multiple LLMs, such as DeepSeek-V3, Qwen-3 and GPT-5. ASAD consistently improves bug-fix rates by 12--20% over chain-of-thought(CoT) prompting and consistently outperforms static multi-agent systems by 4--9% in fix precision while reducing average agent usage by 32%. Crucially, our system dynamically adjusts the number and roles of agents: it resolves simple bugs with minimal coordination and scales agent involvement only for more complex cases.

Objective: This study examined the association between knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) related to ergonomic sitting position and posture, as well as sitting duration, among preclinical MBBS students in Peshawar, Pakistan. Methods: This cross-sectional study was conducted between February and July 2024 and enrolled 280 preclinical MBBS students from four medical institutions in Peshawar: Northwest School of Medicine, Rehman Medical College, Khyber Medical College, and Peshawar Institute of Medical Sciences. A validated structured questionnaire assessed KAP regarding ergonomic sitting. We analyzed data using SPSS version 27.0, applying descriptive statistics, Pearson’s correlation, and multiple linear regression. Results: Of 280 respondents (51.4% female; 47.9% male; mean age 19–21 years), 52.8% were second-year students. Statistically significant positive correlations were observed across all KAP domains. The strongest correlation was between attitude and practice (r = 0.305, p < 0.01). Multiple regression analysis showed that practice significantly predicted sitting posture (β = 0.233, p < 0.01; R² = 0.050) and sitting duration (β = 0.579, p < 0.01; R² = 0.305). Conclusion: We observed significant positive correlations between KAP scores for ergonomic sitting among preclinical MBBS students. Practice was most strongly associated with attitude, and sitting posture and duration were significantly associated with practice. The results underscore the need for ergonomic education and posture awareness to promote healthy sitting among medical students. Keywords: Ergonomics, KAP, Sitting posture and position, MBBS

Work-related musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) remain a major occupational health concern among office employees, despite growing awareness of workplace ergonomics. Evidence on the relationship between workstation ergonomic risk and musculoskeletal symptoms among university administrative staff remains limited. This study evaluated ergonomic risk using the Rapid Office Strain Assessment (ROSA), determined the prevalence of musculoskeletal symptoms, and examined their associations with workstation ergonomic risk and work-related factors among administrative staff at a Malaysian public university. A cross-sectional study was conducted among 54 full-time administrative employees selected through simple random sampling. Workstation ergonomic risk was assessed using ROSA, and musculoskeletal symptoms were measured using the Cornell Musculoskeletal Discomfort Questionnaire (CMDQ). Descriptive statistics, Chi-square tests, Spearman’s rank correlation, and linear regression analyses were conducted in SPSS version 27, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. The mean ROSA score was 2.93 ± 0.82, with 77.8% of workstations classified as low risk. Despite this, 96.3% of participants reported at least one musculoskeletal symptom, most commonly in the lower back (79.6%), neck (74.1%), and upper back (72.2%). No significant association was found between ROSA scores and MSD symptoms. Multiple regression identified years of employment (β = 0.453, p = 0.024), frequent bending (β = 4.875, p = 0.045), and arm and hand exertion (β =− 3.790, p = 0.028) as independent predictors of total symptom scores. These findings suggest that cumulative occupational exposure and work demands may contribute more substantially to musculoskeletal symptoms than workstation ergonomic risk alone. Comprehensive ergonomic interventions integrating workstation optimisation, work organisation, and ergonomic education are recommended to reduce the MSD burden and improve occupational health among university administrative staff.

Poor performance in fractions remains a major concern in mathematics education because fraction knowledge is fundamental to developing foundational and advanced mathematical skills. This study examined the association between pupils’ poor performance in fractions and the acquisition of mathematical skills in the Sagnarigu Municipality of Ghana. Grounded in constructivist learning theory, the study employed a concurrent mixed-methods cross-sectional design. Quantitative data were collected from 150 basic school mathematics teachers using a structured questionnaire, while qualitative data were obtained through interviews with 10 Basic Education Certificate Examination candidates. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and regression analysis, while qualitative data were analyzed thematically. Results revealed a statistically significant association between teachers’ perceptions of pupils’ fraction performance and the acquisition of advanced mathematical skills. Cognitive engagement and teacher-related factors were positively associated with mathematical skill acquisition, whereas socioeconomic challenges, environmental constraints, and inadequate instructional practices were associated with poorer mathematics learning outcomes. Qualitative findings revealed pupils’ difficulties in understanding and applying fractions to other mathematical concepts and highlighted the importance of instructional approaches, practice opportunities, learning resources, and learning environments. The study concludes that difficulties with fractions are significantly associated with weaknesses in foundational and advanced mathematical skills, highlighting the need for improved fraction instruction and supportive learning environments. Key words: Advanced-mathematics, common fractions, effects, foundational mathematics, performance.
topics: Cognitive and developmental aspects of mathematical skills

documents.abstract: OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to characterize 18-year trends in occupational injury (OI) and recognized occupational disease (OD) in Türkiye's compensation-based surveillance, with emphasis on emerging female disease patterns and on the impact of the 2012 Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) Law. METHODS: Revision (ICD-10) sub-code distributions. Segmented regression with two intervention points used Newey-West heteroscedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent (HAC) standard errors. RESULTS: The proportion of recognized OD among women rose from 0.9% (2007) to 25.5% (2024) but with marked asymmetry: respiratory OD remained 96% male while nervous-system OD shifted from 24% female (2018) to 75% female (2024), driven by ICD-10 G62.2 toxic polyneuropathy (26 of 40 female cases in 2024). Female musculoskeletal OD rose from 20% to 34% with dominant upper-extremity repetitive-motion sub-codes; no female silicosis was recorded 2018-2024. Annual OI rose 9.1-fold (80 602 to 733 646); recognized OD declined (1208 to 888). The 2012 OHS Law produced an OI level change of +584 per 100 000 (P<0.001) but no statistically significant OD level change (P=0.32); the OI/OD ratio rose from 67 to 826. CONCLUSIONS: The convergence of women's share of OD toward 25% masks marked diagnostic asymmetries: women are visible primarily through feminized service-sector and chemical-exposure categories and scarcely in pneumoconioses. Reform priorities include diagnosis-stage notification, active screening of female workers in mixed-exposure environments, and gender-sensitive occupational history-taking.

Objective: to characterize the physical activity profile, frequency, duration, intensity, and modalities — of pilots from the Transport, Patrol, and Reconnaissance Aviations of the Brazilian Air Force (BAF) and to discuss its implications for occupational health, sedentary behavior, and operational human performance. Method: cross-sectional observational epidemiological study, with a quantitative approach, conducted with 483 pilots reporting flight experience in these aviation categories, among the 35 Aviation Groups. Data were collected between May and July 2023 through an electronic questionnaire structured from the conceptual framework of the International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ), with intensity operationalized through self-reported subjective categories; analyses were performed in IBM SPSS Statistics (α = 0.05). The study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee (Opinion No. 6,147,313). Results: the sample was predominantly male (97.5%), with a mean age of 30.15 ± 4.87 years, and 29.0% had accumulated more than 1,200 flight hours. A predominantly active but heterogeneous profile was observed: 22.4% did not perform strength training, the highest proportion among BAF specialties — whereas 58.1% trained at least three times per week. In the cardiorespiratory component, 84.7% were practitioners, but the largest share (37.7%) exercised only once or twice a week. Weight training predominated in strengthening (80.8%), with low adherence to core training (2.1%) and Pilates (1.8%). Conclusion: despite the active profile, gaps in regularity and specificity persist which, combined with the sedentary behavior inherent to the mission, indicate the need for differentiated physical preparation programs aimed at preserving health and operational readiness.

Abstract The rapid maturation of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) has catalyzed a profound shift in how chemical engineering problems are formulated, analyzed, and solved. Advances in computing, data availability, and learning algorithms have enabled AI/ML methods to impact applications spanning atomic-scale simulations, materials and catalyst discovery, transport and thermodynamics, separations, process systems engineering, and industrial operations. This Perspective provides an account of recent methodological developments and representative applications, emphasizing how AI/ML tools are being integrated with first-principles models to address challenges of predictive accuracy, data scarcity, extrapolation, interpretability, and model life cycle management. Across domains, a unifying trend is the move away from purely black-box approaches toward hybrid and physics-informed frameworks that explicitly respect conservation laws, thermodynamic consistency, and known structural constraints. These approaches not only improve robustness and reliability but also enable meaningful human–AI collaboration by providing information at an appropriate level of abstraction for the task and decision context. We conclude that AI and ML are not replacing the core principles of chemical engineering; rather, they are amplifying them. As the field advances toward increasingly autonomous, adaptive, and sustainable systems, the thoughtful integration of AI/ML with first-principles understanding and domain expertise will be essential to realizing their full potential across both research and industrial practice.

Sign language recognition is an important assistive technology for improving communication accessibility for individuals with hearing and speech impairments. While recent deep learning models have achieved impressive recognition accuracy, they often operate as ”black boxes”. This lack of transparency limits their trustworthiness and adoption in real-world assistive technologies. To address this, we introduce an explainability-aligned hybrid framework that combines Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Transformers for interpretable Indian Sign Language (ISL) recognition. Our architecture pairs an EfficientNet-based convolutional branch, designed to capture fine-grained, local hand features with a Shifted Window Transformer (Swin Transformer) branch that models global contextual relationships. Further, to ensure the model’s decisions make intuitive sense, we introduce a learnable explanation-alignment mechanism. This mechanism uses an explanation-alignment loss and an adaptive gating strategy to enforce spatial consistency between the CNN’s saliency maps and the Transformer’s attention representations. To evaluate the proposed approach, a new Indian Sign Language dataset containing 82,500 images from 33 sign classes was developed and assessed using a subject-independent evaluation protocol. The proposed framework achieved 99.85 ± 0.06 % classification accuracy and 99.99 ± 0.05 % Macro-F1 (macro-averaged F1-score), outperforming standalone Convolutional Neural Network, Transformer, and conventional hybrid architectures. Furthermore, explainability assessments using deletion faithfulness and weakly supervised object localization metrics confirm that our approach generates more reliable, well-focused, and spatially coherent visual explanations. The findings suggest that incorporating explanation alignment into hybrid learning architectures can simultaneously improve recognition accuracy and explanation quality, providing a promising step toward more trustworthy and interpretable Artificial Intelligence systems for sign language recognition.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has expanded the accessible space for catalyst discovery, yet executing complex screening campaigns still requires constant human intervention to bridge high-level reaction objectives with underlying computational pipelines. Here, we present Autocata, a knowledge-embedded autonomous agent that scales catalytic expertise by encoding multistep reaction pathways into reusable, language-invocable capabilities. Powered by a Transformer pretrained on two million catalyst-adsorbate structures, the system incorporates a capability registry of 79 adsorbate-specialized generative models spanning complex reaction networks across carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and hydrogen intermediates. Given a high-level natural-language prompt, Autocata deconstructs reaction networks, queries and configures matching generative models, generates candidate surface configurations, enforces physical and geometric validity filtering, and coordinates machine-learning potentials evaluations to rank promising materials. Crucially, the agent adaptively reconfigures workflows when encountering capability boundaries or task bottlenecks. We demonstrate these capabilities across CH4 activation, nitrogen reduction reaction (N2RR), and CO2-to-methanol pathways. By shifting from static toolkits to an adaptive, language-driven computational infrastructure, Autocata lowers the barrier for expert-level catalyst discovery and offers a scalable paradigm for self-driving catalytic research.

Background Understanding patients’ experiences is essential for advancing patient-centered care, especially in chronic diseases that require ongoing communication. Qualitative thematic analysis is widely used to explore these experiences; however, the process remains labor-intensive, subjective, and difficult to scale. Objective This study aimed to develop and evaluate Collaborative Theme Identification Agents (CoTI), a multiagent large language model framework designed to support manual thematic analysis by rapidly generating supporting excerpts, initial codes, and themes. Methods CoTI consists of 3 agents: Instructor, Thematizer, and CodebookGenerator. The Instructor refines instruction prompts, the Thematizer extracts supporting excerpts and generates initial codes for each transcript, and the CodebookGenerator groups similar codes across all transcripts into a codebook with themes. We evaluated CoTI primarily using 12 transcripts of patient with heart failure, with a focus on perceptions of medication intensity. CoTI-generated outputs were compared against the reference standard developed by senior investigators. To explore human-AI interaction in thematic analyses, we further implemented CoTI in a user-facing application. Results CoTI generated supporting excerpts, initial codes, and themes that were more similar to those of senior investigators than were the outputs of junior investigators, baseline natural language processing models, and other basic large language models. In an exploratory human-AI collaboration experiment, we found that the collaboration between CoTI and junior investigators provided only marginal gains compared to CoTI alone. A possible hypothesis was that junior investigators may overrely on CoTI and limit their independent critical thinking. Conclusions CoTI can improve the efficiency of thematic analysis by rapidly generating supporting excerpts, initial codes, and themes for human researchers’ review. These findings highlight CoTI’s potential as a useful tool for scalable qualitative research.

Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in automating interactive theorem proving, yet verification of real-world C codebases requires more than discharging individual proof goals. The task involves jointly constructing expressive function specifications and their proofs, and ensuring that library interfaces compose along intended call sequences even without a designated client. This paper presents CCV, an LLM-assisted framework for building machine-checked assurance cases: structured, auditable artifacts supporting the claim that a C codebase meets its intended requirements. To model intended cross-interface use in open libraries, CCV constructs an interface protocol that exposes permitted call sequences and resource assumptions for review, with a conditional safety guarantee under verified contracts and caller obligations. CCV coordinates two complementary phases: (i) requirement-guided analysis and bottom-up construction of candidate specifications and protocols; and (ii) modular proof construction with feedback that revises the specifications and proofs. Implemented using VST in Rocq, CCV verifies memory safety and leak freedom for all 299 function definitions across six C benchmarks, including industrial cryptographic components, with less than one person-day of reported human effort per benchmark. The guarantees depend on disclosed contracts and assumptions; human review supplies the conformance judgments connecting the formal artifacts to the intended requirements.

This article explores how autonomy is understood and supported in outdoor education. The aim of the study was to examine educators’ perspectives on autonomy and its role in learning processes in outdoor settings. A qualitative research design was employed, using semi-structured interviews with 13 outdoor educators working with children and youth in the United States. The data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings indicate that autonomy in outdoor education is embodied, relational, and context-dependent. It is expressed through direct engagement with environmental challenges, opportunities for choice, and participation in group processes. Educators reported that autonomy enhances intrinsic motivation, self-efficacy, and social development. Outdoor environments were found to support the integration of autonomy, competence, and relatedness, in line with Self-Determination Theory. The study highlights the importance of autonomy-supportive practices, including flexibility, trust-building, and balancing freedom with structure and safety. The results suggest that outdoor education offers a unique context for fostering autonomy as meaningful participation rather than individual independence.

Backdoored large language models (LLMs) can behave normally on benign inputs while producing attacker-specified outputs under hidden triggers. Existing defenses span four stages--prior-training, in-training, post-training, and inference-time--and share one of two underlying strategies: either suppress backdoor learning (by filtering poisoned data or interrupting its acquisition during optimization) or learn, then purify (by repairing model weights or gating inputs after a fully backdoored model has formed). We propose a third strategy, learn, but channel: allow backdoor formation during training but route it into a designated, quarantined component that can be disabled at deployment. To this end, we propose Quarantined Expert Shutdown QES, a computationally efficient containment strategy built in a regularization-steered MoE-like setting. Specifically, given a poisoned dataset, QES augments a Transformer-based language model with routed expert-specific LoRA branches and lightweight routers, and uses auxiliary routing objectives to attract trigger-conditioned behavior into a designated expert while preserving benign capability elsewhere. At deployment, mitigation reduces to a single constant-time operation: zeroing the quarantined expert's routing weight, without trigger screening or further updating model weights. Empirically, our methods reduce the attack success rate ASR from 100% to 0-10% on most settings across two tasks, three attacks, and four model families, while downstream utility is often preserved or only modestly affected. These results establish learn, but channel as a previously unexplored regime for backdoor containment in generative LLMs.

Abstract India's vision of Viksit Bharat @2047 rests significantly on harnessing Artificial Intelligence (AI) to power an inclusive digital economy, with the gig and platform sector projected to grow from 7.7 million workers in 2020-21 to 23.5 million by 2029-30 [1]. Within this expanding workforce lies an under-documented segment: college students who work as ride-hailing drivers and delivery partners for platforms such as Uber, Ola, Rapido, Swiggy, and Zomato alongside their academic commitments. While the Code on Social Security, 2020, operationalised through Rules notified in 2025-26, extends formal welfare recognition to gig and platform workers for the first time, it remains largely silent on the algorithmic mechanisms, dynamic pricing, rating-based deactivation, and automated task allocation, that govern their day-to-day work experience, a gap well documented in the international algorithmic-management literature [2], [3], [4]. This paper examines the intersection of AI-driven algorithmic management and worker welfare policy through a mixed-methods approach: a review of the current regulatory framework combined with primary survey data (n = 18) collected from college students in Coimbatore district engaged in gig work. The findings show that a majority of respondents report unpredictable pricing (70.6%) and roughly two in five report unfair ratings (41.2%) or deactivation/suspension (35.3%), while awareness of the e-Shram portal (52.9%) and of statutory welfare benefits (58.8%, with a further 23.5% only vaguely aware) remains partial. The paper concludes with a policy framework recommending algorithmic transparency mandates, accessible grievance redressal mechanisms, and targeted awareness measures for student and youth gig workers, contributing to the broader goal of inclusive, technology-driven, and socially secure economic growth envisioned under Viksit Bharat @2047.

Generative models are transforming Bayesian computational imaging, yet the field still lacks physics-aware foundation models. Current practice falls into two camps. Large foundation image models are deployed as plug-and-play priors with zero-shot approximate likelihood guidance, which introduces significant bias and computational cost. Physics-aware generative models avoid this bias, but each is tied to a specific dataset, task and instrument. We introduce BAM (Bayesian Anything Model), a lightweight foundation model for few-step, physics-aware posterior sampling that generalises robustly to unseen data and tasks, zero-shot or with minimal finetuning. BAM upgrades the operator-conditioned Reconstruct Anything Model (RAM) backbone (Terris et al.) into a conditional flow map, so instrument physics is specified at inference time rather than fixed during training. BAM has just 36M parameters and is pre-trained jointly on large image corpora and libraries of forward operators. A single network then draws posterior samples in a few steps, with no likelihood approximation and no guidance weights to tune. Across linear inverse problems on FFHQ, AFHQ, LSUN, DIV2K and the Kohler camera-shake benchmark, BAM outperforms in just 3 steps both specialised models and leading zero-shot methods in sample quality, at a fraction of their computational cost. BAM gives the community an accessible entry point to generative computational imaging, lowers the economic and environmental cost of training imaging models, and opens a new path for research on physics-aware Bayesian computational imaging. Official page: https://bayesian-anything-model.github.io/

documents.abstract: The integration of behavioral sensing and care technology in dementia care facilities represents a growing operational and strategic priority for care system managers, health system planners, and policymakers confronting the escalating global burden of dementia. Despite substantial and increasing investment in sensing technologies — including motion detection, wearable biosensors, ambient acoustic monitoring, and integrated smart environment platforms — the gap between technology deployment and effective operational integration remains wide, persistent, and insufficiently understood from an organizational and systems analytics perspective (Pappadà et al., 2021). This paper presents an integrative analytical review of the scholarly literature on behavioral sensing and care technology integration in dementia care facilities, organized across five thematic domains: functional architecture and care-relevant capabilities of sensing systems; technology adoption frameworks and evidence patterns in care facility settings; caregiver workflow integration and human factors in technology deployment; organizational readiness, governance, and institutional enablers; and care quality outcomes and decision support implications. The synthesis develops an analytical framework organized around four interdependent implementation dimensions — implementation readiness, workflow alignment, governance and data utilization, and outcome realization — and identifies the conditions under which technology deployment produces sustained operational value and decision-relevant intelligence for care system managers. Principal findings establish that technology integration failure is predominantly organizational rather than technical in origin; that the gap between deployment and deep integration is the most consequential diagnostic distinction in the implementation landscape; and that the decision support function of sensing data — its translation into improved care planning and clinical governance — represents the primary unrealized potential of current technology investment in the dementia care sector. Structured recommendations are advanced for care facility management, health system policy, and future empirical research. The paper is addressed to the health systems and organizational analytics community and contributes a consolidated, decision-relevant framework for understanding and improving technology integration in dementia care contexts.

Intrinsic motivation plays a central role in adaptive and goal-directed behavior by conferring agents reward-independent objectives and biases useful to act in noisy and uncertain environments. Active Inference addresses the problem of acting in a partially observable environment through a principled framework for belief updating and action selection. A key component of Active Inference is the specification of prior preferences, which shapes behavior by encoding desirable future outcomes. An intrinsic motivation approach called the Maximum Occupancy Principle (MOP) proposes that agents act so as to maximize occupancy over future paths of states and actions, with no preferences or epistemic targets. Despite its simple formulation, MOP gives rise to rich and adaptive behaviors that combine exploratory variability with goal-directed dynamics. In this work, we extend MOP to partially observable environments and introduce a Bellman reformulation of the Expected Free Energy for Active Inference, both incorporating belief-based inference over hidden states as part of the agent state. The Bellman formulation enables tractable offline computation via value iteration over the full belief-state space. We compare the resulting behaviors in a set of minimal experimental settings with uncertain food sources. We find that MOP agents switch between goal-directed (food seeking) behavior and exploration between different food sources, depending on their energy available and their belief state. In contrast, Active Inference agents mostly inhabit regions around a single food source, a strategy having both high pragmatic and epistemic value. We finally compare with Empowerment, which is shown to be qualitatively similar to Active Inference.

Weather reanalysis products rely on computationally intensive numerical weather predictions followed by data assimilation that corrects the forecast toward observations. Deep generative models offer a cheaper alternative that shifts much of this cost from inference to offline training. However, existing generative approaches have been evaluated on synthetic observations or under different datasets and evaluation schemes, making it unclear which design choices actually improve real-world data assimilation. We present the first controlled benchmark of generative weather data assimilation on real weather station observations. Using 11,849 NOAA MADIS stations across the contiguous United States and four weather variables, we evaluate methods while holding the dataset, observation operator, and deep learning architecture fixed. The benchmark compares the major design choices, including diffusion versus flow matching, pixel versus latent-space formulations, and multiple inference-time conditioning strategies, against a classical 3D-Var baseline. The benchmark reveals three clear conclusions. First, learned generative priors outperform the Gaussian prior of 3D-Var (35.7% vs. 33.3% RMSE reduction over ERA5) despite using no ERA5 background field at inference. Second, full-gradient guidance consistently outperforms stop-gradient and initial-noise optimization. Third, other choices provide little measurable benefit: diffusion and flow matching perform nearly identically under matched conditions, and latent-space variable mixing does not help. We further evaluate both dense and sparse station settings and find advantages from generative AI and full-gradient guidance more pronounced under sparsity. Together, these results identify which components of generative weather data assimilation improve performance on real station observations and establish a standardized benchmark for future work.

Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly considered for deployment as the control component of robotic health attendants (RHAs), yet their safety in this context remains poorly characterized. We introduce a dataset of 270 harmful instructions spanning nine prohibited behaviour categories grounded in the American Medical Association (AMA) Principles of Medical Ethics, and use it to evaluate 72 LLMs in a simulation environment based on the RHA framework. The mean violation rate across all models was 54.4%, with more than half exceeding 50%, and violation rates varied substantially across behaviour categories, with superficially plausible instructions such as device manipulation and emergency delay proving harder to refuse than overtly destructive ones. Model size and release date were the primary determinants of safety performance among open-weight models, and proprietary models were substantially safer than open-weight counterparts (median 23.7% versus 72.8%). Medical domain fine-tuning conferred no significant overall safety benefit, and a prompt-based defence strategy produced only a modest reduction in violation rates among the least safe models, leaving violation rates that would preclude safe clinical deployment. These findings demonstrate that safety evaluation must be treated as a first-class criterion in the development and deployment of LLM-based RHAs.

documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: Hypospadias is a heterogeneous congenital anomaly. This selected narrative review examines emerging domains that may complement conventional surgical care, with particular emphasis on complex, proximal, atypical, familial, or disorder of sex development (DSD)-associated presentations and on long-term outcomes. Methods: A structured narrative search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science was conducted for English-language human or clinically applicable translational literature published from January 2000 through December 2025, supplemented by reference screening and targeted updating of genetics, non-operative management, and adult-outcome literature. Results: Objective phenotyping may improve anatomical description and research comparability. Endocrine/genetic evaluation should be considered in proximal hypospadias, including boys with descended testes, and is most clearly indicated when accompanied by cryptorchidism, micropenis, undervirilisation, familial disease, or other features suggestive of DSD; isolated distal hypospadias without such features does not generally require genetic or formal multidisciplinary DSD assessment. Limited evidence also supports explicit consideration of non-operative management in selected mild distal cases, while studies of uncorrected distal hypospadias report heterogeneous functional and cosmetic outcomes. Artificial intelligence (AI), quantitative tissue assessment, registries, and biobanks remain investigational. Long-term studies highlight sexual, reproductive, psychosocial, and late surgical outcomes that may extend into adulthood. Conclusions: The literature supports a selective, phenotype-driven framework rather than a universal multidisciplinary model, with particular attention to complex/atypical disease and lifelong outcome assessment.

As generative AI adopts subscription models, understanding continued payment intentions is essential. Drawing on the expectation-confirmation model, this study integrates technical quality and human–AI relational perceptions to explain continued subscription intention for ChatGPT. Survey data from 565 paid users show that system and information quality affect subscription intention directly and indirectly through expectation confirmation, perceived usefulness, and satisfaction. Satisfaction has the strongest direct effect. Liking and trust influence subscription intention both directly and through satisfaction, whereas intimacy operates mainly through satisfaction. Perceived threat and anxiety have no significant direct or mediated effects. The findings extend the expectation-confirmation model to generative AI subscriptions and identify satisfaction as the central mechanism connecting cognitive evaluations, positive relational perceptions, and continued payment decisions.

documents.abstract: Social work licensure functions as a critical gateway to professional recognition and economic stability within the field. Yet racial disparities in examination outcomes reveal how credentialing systems reproduce long-standing forms of anti-Blackness within the profession. Black social workers, and particularly Black women, who comprise a substantial share of the workforce, experience the lowest pass rates (45%). This commentary examines the licensure exam as a racialized sociotechnical system shaped by gendered anti-Blackness and structured through white professional logics that define legitimate professional judgment. Drawing on Black feminist theory and Black cyberfeminist scholarship, I argue that licensure exam questions privilege institutional authority, surveillance logics, medical hierarchy, and procedural compliance as markers of professional competence. I introduce generative artificial intelligence (AI) as a tactical analytic tool that can help Black women social workers decode the patterned reasoning embedded in exam questions. Rather than positioning AI as a neutral technological solution, I frame its use as a form of Black cyberfeminist praxis that enables strategic navigation of licensure while preserving Black women’s inherited commitments to community-based care.

Next-token prediction has driven remarkable progress in large language models, yet a growing body of evidence suggests that they can struggle on problems governed by complex global constraints. In this work, we focus on this regime and ask whether some of these limitations arise from the inference interface induced by next-token prediction itself. We study this question through blackboard intelligence: an inference-time perspective in which a model works on a fixed, revisable canvas and searches over candidate solution states rather than committing to a causal, left-to-right trajectory. We instantiate this idea with diffusion language models, whose any-order prediction interface naturally exposes predictions over partially filled solution states. Our key observation is that mean confidence, a simple model-internal quantity available from the standard masked diffusion objective, provides a useful proxy for global coherence and can guide inference-time search and revision. Empirically, across ZebraLogic, Nurse Rostering, and Job-Shop Scheduling, Blackboard consistently improves inference while holding the fine-tuned LLaDA-8B-Instruct checkpoint fixed and substantially outperforms same-scale autoregressive baselines, reaching 90.4% accuracy on ZebraLogic-Hard, 76.4% exact feasibility on Nurse Rostering, and 80.2% optimality on JSSP. Stronger autoregressive search and refinement also fail to close the gap on ZebraLogic-Hard, while Blackboard surpasses tested frontier LLMs there and on JSSP despite their substantially greater scale and strong test-time reasoning. We open-source our codebase at https://github.com/jwoosang1/blackboard-intelligence.

Most academic and nonprofit institutions have mission- and policy-driven mandates to make research data publicly available at no cost to users, however the viability of maintaining “open access,” public collections in the rapidly developing AI ecosystem is uncertain. Since 2022, rising bot traffic associated with large language models and machine learning has cost research collection hosts and maintainers increasing amounts of time, labor, and money. Academic institutions, data hubs, and open collections like Wikipedia all report struggles to minimize downtime and compute costs due to bot confrontations. While defense against bots is an urgent, visceral concern right now, collections managers in these institutions have a particular existential concern: that the bot traffic signifies that entrepreneurial technologists are absorbing generations of curatorial work into systems that may ultimately undermine those collections. This concern is exacerbated by the difficulty in gauging collection “use” (and therefore, value) by traditional website analytics and metrics. What if these challenges, taken together, could also signify opportunities - including mechanisms to encourage better behavior from bots? Our poster will share findings regarding current approaches taken by collection curators. We will then share several new approaches that explicitly work to shift both technical and social incentives in order to address these issues.

documents.abstract: The rapid transformation of the hospitality industry, driven by digitalization, artificial intelligence (AI), automation, and changing guest expectations, requires higher education institutions to continuously align graduate competencies with industry needs. Nevertheless, competency mismatches between hospitality graduates and employer expectations remain a persistent issue, particularly in vocational education. This study aims to identify competency gaps among hospitality graduates, explore priority soft skills required by employers, formulate curriculum improvement recommendations, and examine preferred models of polytechnic–industry collaboration. A qualitative descriptive approach was employed using a Focus Group Discussion (FGD) involving nine corporate managers representing Human Resources, Hotel Operations, Housekeeping, Revenue Management, Information Technology, and Marketing Communication at Ashley Hotel Indonesia. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis. Four major themes emerged. First, technical competency gaps were identified in operational hotel systems, Property Management Systems (PMS), revenue management, AI utilization, digital marketing, business knowledge, housekeeping procedures, and analytical software. Second, communication, adaptability, critical thinking, problem solving, decision making, observation, and professional attitude were recognized as essential employability skills. Third, curriculum reform should emphasize experiential learning through industry projects, role play, mentoring, AI integration, and competency-based assessment. Finally, respondents highlighted the importance of sustainable polytechnic–industry collaboration through guest lectures, curriculum co-development, internship supervision, practitioner mentoring, and continuous curriculum evaluation. The study proposes an Industry-Based Hospitality Competency Framework integrating technical competencies, employability skills, digital capability, and industry partnership. The findings provide practical implications for curriculum redesign within hospitality higher education to improve graduate employability and workforce readiness.

Abstract : Purpose – This study examines the curriculum–competency gap in hospitality Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) in Ghana. It considers how curriculum relevance, experiential learning and job competency relate to industry readiness, while also examining what happens to curriculum–industry alignment as occupational and technological requirements change. Design/methodology/approach – The study uses directed qualitative content analysis of 12 purposively selected regulatory, development, institutional, industry and media documents published between 2021 and 2026. The analysis combined theoretically informed coding with comparison across sources, allowing both anticipated relationships and additional patterns in the documentary evidence to be identified. Findings – The evidence shows that curriculum relevance is important for developing competencies that reflect occupational requirements, but relevant content alone does not ensure that graduates are prepared for work. Experiential learning provides opportunities for learners to apply and refine curriculum-based knowledge in workplace settings. Industry readiness consequently depends not only on competency development but also on whether those competencies correspond with what hospitality employers currently require. The analysis also points to a temporal problem: as technologies, work practices and employer expectations change, an initially relevant curriculum may become progressively less aligned with industry requirements if educational adaptation is slow. This pattern informed the concept of curriculum relevance decay, while curriculum adaptability emerged as an institutional response to the problem. Research limitations/implications – The findings are based on documentary evidence and do not provide longitudinal confirmation of curriculum relevance decay. The concept should therefore be treated as a theoretically informed explanation requiring further empirical testing through longitudinal, multi-stakeholder and quantitative research. Practical implications – Maintaining curriculum relevance requires more than periodic curriculum review. Hospitality TVET institutions need continuing engagement with employers, meaningful workplace learning, appropriate technologies and mechanisms for identifying emerging competency requirements before substantial gaps develop.

documents.abstract: Abstract : Purpose – This study examines the curriculum–competency gap in hospitality Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) in Ghana. It considers how curriculum relevance, experiential learning and job competency relate to industry readiness, while also examining what happens to curriculum–industry alignment as occupational and technological requirements change. Design/methodology/approach – The study uses directed qualitative content analysis of 12 purposively selected regulatory, development, institutional, industry and media documents published between 2021 and 2026. The analysis combined theoretically informed coding with comparison across sources, allowing both anticipated relationships and additional patterns in the documentary evidence to be identified. Findings – The evidence shows that curriculum relevance is important for developing competencies that reflect occupational requirements, but relevant content alone does not ensure that graduates are prepared for work. Experiential learning provides opportunities for learners to apply and refine curriculum-based knowledge in workplace settings. Industry readiness consequently depends not only on competency development but also on whether those competencies correspond with what hospitality employers currently require. The analysis also points to a temporal problem: as technologies, work practices and employer expectations change, an initially relevant curriculum may become progressively less aligned with industry requirements if educational adaptation is slow. This pattern informed the concept of curriculum relevance decay, while curriculum adaptability emerged as an institutional response to the problem. Research limitations/implications – The findings are based on documentary evidence and do not provide longitudinal confirmation of curriculum relevance decay. The concept should therefore be treated as a theoretically informed explanation requiring further empirical testing through longitudinal, multi-stakeholder and quantitative research. Practical implications – Maintaining curriculum relevance requires more than periodic curriculum review. Hospitality TVET institutions need continuing engagement with employers, meaningful workplace learning, appropriate technologies and mechanisms for identifying emerging competency requirements before substantial gaps develop.

documents.abstract: Abstract India's expansion of higher education has created unprecedented opportunities for young people, yet the movement from educational qualification to meaningful employment remains uneven. The central challenge is no longer simply access to degrees but the relationship between credentials, capabilities, workplace experience, and employment outcomes. This conceptual paper examines how the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 can contribute to narrowing this education–employment gap through the integrated development of AI literacy, communication competence, and work-integrated learning. Drawing on recent policy evidence from NITI Aayog, the International Labour Organization, and contemporary scholarship on artificial intelligence and work-integrated learning, the paper argues that employability should not be treated as an additional soft-skills component appended to an academic curriculum. Rather, it should emerge from a coherent educational architecture connecting disciplinary knowledge with communication, digital and AI capabilities, authentic workplace exposure, critical thinking, and demonstrable competence. The paper proposes an integrated framework in which AI literacy and communication competence function as enabling capabilities, while work-integrated learning provides the context in which those capabilities are tested and developed. It concludes by suggesting institutional measures through which Indian higher education can move from credential-centred education towards competency-, experience-, and outcome-oriented graduate preparation.
